section.title: As the Deer Pants for Water
section.sectionRationale: The opening psalm of Book II, Psalms 42-72, this is the first of the Korahite psalms and forms one continuous poem with Psalm 43, bound together by the same refrain repeated three times. It models the soul talking to itself rather than simply listening to itself in downcast despair, longing for God as a deer longs for water.
section.thesis: The psalmist's soul thirsts for the living God as a deer thirsts for water, and though downcast and taunted by enemies who ask 'Where is your God?', he preaches hope to his own soul, refusing despair and choosing to wait for God's salvation.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the soul's thirst for God amid tears and taunts, verses 1-4; the first refrain of self-address, remembering God even from the depths, verses 5-8; and the return of the taunt met again by the same refrain of hope, verses 9-11.

units.label: As the deer pants for streams of water
units.note: the soul's thirst amid tears and taunts

verses.text: As the deer {{arag|pants}} for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God.
My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear in God's presence?
My tears have been my food both day and night, while men ask me all day long, "Where is your God?"
These things come to mind as I pour out my soul: how I walked with the multitude, leading the procession to the house of God with shouts of joy and praise.

units.label: Why are you downcast, O my soul

verses.text: Why are you {{shachach|downcast}}, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence.
O my God, my soul despairs within me. Therefore I remember You from the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon, even from Mount Mizar.
Deep calls to deep in the roar of Your waterfalls; all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me.

The LORD decrees His loving devotion by day, and at night His song is with me 
as a prayer to the God of my life.

units.label: I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God
units.note: the taunt returns, and so does hope

verses.text: I say to God my Rock, "Why have You forgotten me? Why must I walk in sorrow because of the enemy's oppression?"
Like the crushing of my bones, my enemies taunt me, while they say to me all day long, "Where is your God?"
Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God.

arag.gloss: To pant or long intensely, used only here and in Joel 1:20 of animals crying out for water in drought, a physical, desperate longing rather than a mild wish, describing the soul's craving for God as bodily thirst.

shachach.gloss: Bowed down, downcast, or sunk low, from a root meaning to bow or crouch. The psalmist addresses his own soul directly by name in this state, preaching to it rather than merely listening to its despair.

basic.context: Likely written by someone exiled or far from the Jerusalem temple, remembering days of leading festival processions with shouts of joy, this psalmist now weeps day and night while enemies taunt him, 'Where is your God?' Rather than surrender to despair, he turns and speaks directly to his own soul, commanding it to hope in God, a refrain repeated at the end of each movement.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm models a crucial spiritual discipline: talking to oneself rather than simply listening to oneself. The psalmist does not deny his downcast, despairing feelings, but interrogates them and answers them with truth about God, showing that honest lament and disciplined hope are not opposites.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalmist's longing is arag, the intense panting of a thirst-stricken animal, used elsewhere only of creatures crying out in drought, Joel 1:20, picturing desperate physical need rather than casual desire. His soul is shachach, bowed down or sunk low, which he directly addresses and commands rather than simply obeying its despair.
basic.typology: The psalmist's soul crushed with sorrow while enemies taunt 'Where is your God?' anticipates Christ's own anguish, His soul 'deeply grieved, to the point of death,' Matthew 26:38, and the mockery He endured on the cross, 'He trusts in God; let God rescue Him now,' Matthew 27:43, a nearly identical taunt.
basic.christ: The taunt hurled at the psalmist, 'Where is your God?', anticipates the almost identical mockery hurled at Christ on the cross, 'He trusts in God; let God rescue Him now if He wants Him,' Matthew 27:43. Jesus Himself entered this psalm's very anguish, His soul deeply grieved even to death, Matthew 26:38, yet, like the psalmist, moved through that darkness toward resurrection praise, the pattern this psalm's refrain, 'I will yet praise Him,' anticipates and secures for all who are in Him.
basic.god: God is shown as the living water for which the soul thirsts, present even in the roar of overwhelming waves, His loving devotion decreed by day and His song given even in the darkest night.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 27:43 records mockers taunting Jesus on the cross with words strikingly similar to this psalm's 'Where is your God?'. Matthew 26:38 shows Jesus's own soul deeply grieved, echoing this psalm's downcast soul. John 7:37-38 pictures Jesus offering living water to all who thirst, answering this psalm's central longing.
basic.oneStory: The psalmist's thirsting soul, downcast yet preaching hope to itself amid taunts asking 'Where is your God?', anticipates Christ, who entered this very anguish on the cross, mocked with nearly identical words, yet who is Himself the living water for which every thirsty soul longs and the ground of the hope this psalm refuses to relinquish.

context.literary:
Psalms 42 and 43 are one poem in three stanzas, and the refrain is the hinge of each: 42:5, 42:11 and 43:5. The refrain is a question followed by a command, then a promise. The poet interrogates his own soul, orders it to wait, and tells it what it will one day do. Around that fixed line the stanzas circle rather than climb. Each begins in thirst or grief, brushes against memory of the sanctuary, and lands on the taunt or the plea that leads back to the refrain. Psalm 43 breaks the circle at last, because there the memory turns into a request to be taken home, 43:3-4.

The first stanza, 42:1-5, is built on two pictures of the body. The deer pants, and the tears become food, verse 3. The psalmist eats grief where he should be eating festival meat, and the word for his hunger is the word for his inmost self. Verse 4 is a sudden flashback set off by the phrase 'These things come to mind', and it is the only stretch in the poem written in the past tense of joy.

The second stanza, 42:6-11, is the most concentrated poetry. Water carries the whole of it: the Jordan, the peaks of Hermon, the waterfalls, the breakers and the waves. The Lord's loving devotion is 'decreed' by day and His song is with the poet at night, verse 8, a small chiasm of day and night that cuts across the flood imagery. Verse 9 then turns to the second person and dares to say 'Why have You forgotten me?' The taunt of verse 3 returns word for word in verse 10, so the psalm frames its grief with the same mocking question.

The poet moves between speaking to God, speaking about God and speaking to himself. Only the refrain addresses the soul, and it always sits at the end of the stanza, as if prayer must pass through self-address before it can rest.
context.historical:
The heading names the sons of Korah. The Korahites were Levites, and Chronicles remembers them as gatekeepers and singers in the house of the Lord, 1 Chronicles 9:19 and 2 Chronicles 20:19. That fits a poet who once led a festival procession and now mourns his exclusion from it. The heading also calls the psalm a maskil, which the BSB footnote takes to be a musical or liturgical term.

The geography of verse 6 places the singer in the far north. The Jordan rises at the foot of Mount Hermon, whose snowy ridge stands above the sources at Dan and Caesarea Philippi, and 'Mount Mizar' is a hill otherwise unknown to us. The poet is therefore either exiled in the north, deported with the captives of Israel or Judah, or travelling there for some reason the text does not give. He hears water pouring off the mountain and thinks of sanctuary. The details are too thin to fix a date, and the psalm is better read as a pattern of many exiles than pinned to one.

The taunt 'Where is your God?' was a real weapon in the ancient world. A god was thought to be present in his temple and to fight for his people, so a people dragged far from the temple and defeated by their enemies looked abandoned by their god. The same jeer appears in Psalm 79:10 and Joel 2:17, and it fell on the exiles of Judah with special force after the temple was burned. The psalmist meets it with two responses. He remembers how the worshipping crowd looked, verse 4, and he tells his soul that the present is not the last word, verse 5.

The Levite's grief is also about sound. He led the crowd 'with shouts of joy and praise', and the thing he misses is the voice of a gathered people. Isolation from the assembly is part of the pain.
context.canonical:
Psalm 42 opens Book II of the Psalter, which runs to Psalm 72 and begins with a run of Korahite psalms, 42 to 49. Book I, Psalms 1 to 41, ended with a doxology, so the reader arrives at 42 after a pause, and lands in longing rather than praise. Book II is also the part of the Psalter in which the name Elohim, God, is used far more than the covenant name, a feature scholars have noticed across Psalms 42 to 83. The refrain of this poem is built on that name, 'Put your hope in God'.

The psalm draws on earlier Scripture in several places. The verb for the deer's panting is used of the wild beasts in Joel 1:20, 'Even the beasts of the field pant for You', where drought is the setting. The waves and breakers of verse 7 are repeated almost exactly in Jonah's prayer from inside the fish, Jonah 2:3, 'all Your breakers and waves swept over me'. Jonah's words show how readily later worshippers borrowed this psalm's sea imagery for their own distress.

The thirst of verse 2 belongs to a family of psalms of yearning. David says in Psalm 63:1 that his soul thirsts in a dry and weary land, and another Korahite, in Psalm 84:2, says that his soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord and cries out for the living God. The three passages share the idea that the truest desire is for God Himself, not for His gifts.

The New Testament takes up the thirst and the troubled soul. Jesus cries at the feast, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink', John 7:37, and in Gethsemane His soul is consumed with sorrow, Matthew 26:38. The Bible ends with the answer to the poet's question, 'When shall I come and appear in God's presence?', when God's people 'will see His face', Revelation 22:4.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet is not offering a theory of depression or a formula for recovery. He is composing a prayer for the choir, a text the whole community will sing, and he shapes it so that singing it teaches the singer how to grieve without losing faith. The refrain is a script. Worshippers who cannot yet feel hope are given words to say to their own hearts until the feeling catches up.

He wants the hearers to see three things. First, longing for God is not weakness but the mark of a living soul; the deer is desperate because the water is life. Second, memory is a tool, not a trap. He does not use the sanctuary days to torment himself but to remind his soul what God is like, and verse 6 says as much: 'Therefore I remember You'. Third, doubt can be spoken aloud to God. The 'Why have You forgotten me?' of verse 9 sits beside 'my Rock' in the same breath, so complaint and confidence share one sentence.

A Levite writing for other Levites and for pilgrims would also want the community to keep a place for the absent. The psalm reminds those in the assembly that some worshippers are far off, and that their thirst is real. It tells the exiles that they are not forgotten by the singers at home, and the hearers that hope is a duty as well as a hope.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes one person's experience of distance from God. It does not promise that every believer will pass through the same sequence, or that reciting the refrain will lift the mood by the third repetition. Notice that the poem ends in Psalm 43 with the same line it used twice before, and the sorrow has not been argued away. Honest readers should not turn the psalm into a rule such as 'if you keep telling yourself to hope, your feelings will change'.

What the text does prescribe by its shape is the practice of turning grief into address. The poet speaks to God, to himself and about God, and he does not stay silent. It is fair to take that as a pattern for prayer. It is also fair to learn from the way he separates the soul from the self who commands it, and to see that Scripture treats troubled feelings as something to be answered with truth, not merely obeyed or suppressed.

The taunt, the tears and the sea are described, not commanded. Nothing in the psalm tells the sufferer to seek suffering, or to treat enemies' mockery as a sign of holiness. Where the psalm is picked up in the New Testament, it is Christ who enters the anguish on our behalf, and the believer's comfort comes from that fact and not from the sufferer's own achievement of hope.

debates.question: Does 'deep calls to deep' in verse 7 describe crushing affliction, or something more positive?

views.label: The deeps are waves of suffering
views.case: The next line settles the tone: 'all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me'. The deep that calls is the chaos water of the sea, one wave answering another, and Jonah 2:3 borrows the same breakers and waves for a drowning man. On this view the poet is saying that trouble comes in layers and that each one summons the next.

views.label: Deep calls to deep as God's depths meeting the psalmist's
views.case: Others hear the depth of human need calling to the depth of God's mercy, and note that the waves are 'Your' waves and that the verse that follows speaks of the Lord's loving devotion. The waters are God's own, so even the flood is within His reach. This reading is popular in devotional use and is compatible with the first.

views.label: An echo of the primeval deep
views.case: The Hebrew word for deep is the word used for the primeval waters of Genesis 1:2. On that reading the psalmist feels returned to pre-creation chaos, and his hope is that the God who ordered the deep will do so again for him.

debates.bearing: The immediate context favours the flood reading, but the ownership language, 'Your waterfalls', 'Your breakers', keeps God in charge of the water. A sound reading holds the two together: the sea is overwhelming and it is His.

debates.question: Where is the psalmist, and how far can we know his circumstances?

views.label: An exile in the far north
views.case: The Jordan and Hermon in verse 6 point to a place at the source of the river. An exile deported there, or a Levite living outside the land during a time of war, would fit the sense of being cut off from the temple and the mocking of foreign captors.

views.label: A pilgrim or a Levite on service or in illness
views.case: Nothing in the psalm demands a deportation. The poet may be a temple singer sent north, or a man in sickness. The phrase 'crushing of my bones' in verse 10 has been read as physical pain.

views.label: An intentionally general voice
views.case: The psalm gives no name, no date and no king. Its details work as poetic images, so that every worshipper who sings it can supply their own place of distance.

debates.bearing: The uncertainty is not a problem. The refrain, the thirst and the taunt are the parts that carry, and the psalm gives us enough about the Jordan to feel its distance without needing to locate it.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb for the deer's longing, arag, has already been noted; the words around it deserve equal attention. In verse 1 the noun for the soul is nephesh, which in ordinary Hebrew also means the throat, the place where thirst is felt. That is why the psalm can move so smoothly from a panting animal to a soul that thirsts, verse 2. The thirst is bodily as well as spiritual. The same word is at work in Psalm 63:1, where the soul thirsts in a waterless land.

The refrain holds three carefully chosen words. The soul is 'downcast', which is the lexicon word shachach, and the 'unease' is a verb built on hamah, a root that describes the roar of the sea and the murmuring of a crowd. The very verb that describes the soul's turmoil is used of waters in Psalm 46:3, 'their waters roar and foam'. The inner storm and the outer sea speak the same language, which prepares for the flood in verse 7. Then comes the command, 'Put your hope', a causative form of yachal, to wait with expectation. It is used in Psalm 130:5, 'in His word I put my hope', and Lamentations 3:24, 'therefore I will hope in Him'. The psalmist does not ask the soul to feel hopeful; he tells it to make itself wait.

In verse 4 the phrase 'I pour out my soul' uses shapak, the verb for pouring out water or blood. Hannah uses the same idiom of her prayer at Shiloh, 1 Samuel 1:15, 'I have poured out my soul before the LORD'. The psalmist pours out his soul in memory, and the sanctuary is at the far end of the image.

Verse 8 speaks of God 'decreeing' His loving devotion. The verb tsavah is the ordinary verb for commanding or appointing. The psalm pictures chesed as something God orders out each day, like a king sending a messenger, so that the sufferer's daily food of tears, verse 3, is matched by a daily provision of covenant love. The BSB footnote to verse 2 notes another reading, 'and see the face of God', which shows the ambiguity of the verb 'appear': in the Hebrew idiom of pilgrimage, to appear before God is to see His face.

The last words of verse 11 and verse 5 differ in the Hebrew text as the BSB renders them. Verse 5 reads 'the salvation of His presence' and verse 11 reads 'my Savior and my God'. The word for salvation is plural in form, a plural of intensity, and the change from 'presence' to 'my God' lets the refrain end at the person rather than the blessing.

typology.type: The taunt 'Where is your God?', verses 3 and 10
typology.fulfillment: The mocking question that pursues the psalmist finds its fullest echo at Calvary. The passers by shake their heads and say, 'He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him', Matthew 27:43, words taken from Psalm 22:8. Both sufferers are told that their trust has proved empty because rescue does not come. In Christ the correspondence deepens. The taunt is answered not by removing the suffering but by the resurrection, Acts 2:24. The type falls short because the psalmist, though faithful, is one sinner among sinners, whereas Christ was wholly innocent and bore the cost of others.

typology.type: The flood that rolls over the singer, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The breakers and waves that pass over the psalmist are used again by Jonah, and Jesus takes Jonah as His sign, Matthew 12:40. The Lord Himself is in a boat swamped by waves, Mark 4:37, and He sleeps, and He commands the sea to be still, Mark 4:39. The picture escalates because the Lord of the waters goes down into the deep of death for three days and rises. The correspondence is with the pattern and not with a prediction: the psalm nowhere says the Messiah will drown. It falls short because the psalmist is only rescued by hope, while Christ is the one who rescues.

typology.type: The thirst for living water, verses 1 and 2
typology.fulfillment: The soul that thirsts for the living God is answered by Jesus at the feast of Tabernacles: 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink', John 7:37-38. He offers the woman at the well water that becomes 'a fount of water springing up to eternal life', John 4:14. The Old Testament longing to appear in God's presence is met in the One who has 'made His dwelling among us', John 1:14. The type is limited because the psalmist could only travel to a building; the believer now receives the Spirit as a spring within, and the full satisfaction awaits the day when 'the Lamb will lead them to springs of living water', Revelation 7:17.

typology.type: The Levite exiled from the procession, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: A man who once led the crowd to the house of God, and is now cut off, reflects Israel's exile from the temple and points ahead to the people who cannot come to the sanctuary. The New Testament shows Christ as the true temple, John 2:19-21, so that access no longer depends on a place. Believers 'have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God', Hebrews 12:22, and the procession is now the whole church gathered around the Lamb. The type is limited by its geography, since the poet is far from a place and the church is near a Person.

study.christ:
The psalm meets Christ first through the taunt. The question 'Where is your God?' is the most direct verbal link to the cross. The crowd at Calvary asks the same thing in different words, and Jesus is treated as a man whom God has left. Yet the link runs deeper than the words. The psalmist's inner state, his soul troubled and bowed, is taken up by Jesus. In Gethsemane His 'soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death', Matthew 26:38, and John records Him saying, 'Now My soul is troubled', John 12:27. Jesus is a man who knew what it is to face turmoil of soul and to bring it to His Father, and Hebrews 4:15 says that He sympathizes with our weaknesses.

The psalm leads to Christ also by answering the thirst. Jesus stands at the feast and calls out, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink', John 7:37. The living God that the deer pants for is not only a deity in a distant sanctuary. He has come near. John 1:14 says that the Word 'made His dwelling among us', using the language of the tabernacle, so the poet's question, 'When shall I come and appear in God's presence?', has an answer in a person one can see and touch. The longing to see God's face is met in the one who says 'Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father', John 14:9.

The psalm also leads to Christ through the refrain of hope. The psalmist promises, 'I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God'. The New Testament shows the one who did this to the end. He trusts God through the flood of death and is raised, Acts 2:24, and Hebrews 12:2 says that for the joy set before Him He endured the cross. What the poet tells his soul to expect, Christ receives.

The reading needs care. Psalm 42 is not a prophecy in the way Psalm 22 is, and the psalmist's guilt or innocence is not the point. The link is one of experience and pattern: a righteous sufferer, an unbelieving taunt, a flood, and a hope that God will vindicate. Christ takes that pattern and fills it, and His people then sing the psalm in Him.
study.god:
The psalm's first claim about God is that He is 'the living God', verse 2. The title is set against the taunt of verse 3. A god who cannot be found in exile is a god of a place; the living God is not bound to the shrine where He is worshipped, and the poet can address Him from the slopes of Hermon. The taunt assumes that God's presence can be measured by circumstances. The psalm replies that His presence is real even when it is not felt, and it shows this by describing His activity in the poet's day and night, verse 8.

The second claim is that God's loving devotion is active and ordered. The Lord 'decrees' it, as a king decrees, and the song that accompanies the singer through the night is His song, not the poet's. This is a striking picture of God as one who sends love into the dark. His chesed is not a mood but an appointment, and it falls in due course by day.

Third, God is Rock. In verse 9 the poet calls Him 'my Rock' in the very sentence in which he charges Him with forgetting him. The word carries steadiness, an unmoving ground beneath the moving water of verse 7. The poem holds two things together that a shallow faith would separate: God is the sovereign owner of the flood, 'Your waterfalls', 'Your breakers', and He is the refuge in the flood. The same hand that permits the waves is the one that stands as rock. The psalm does not explain why, and it does not need to.

Fourth, God is the God of the poet's life, verse 8, the source and preserver of breath and being. Worship in this psalm is therefore not a mood but a relationship with the living one, and the poet does not want gifts from Him; he wants Him.

For worship, the psalm teaches that God welcomes honest speech. He is addressed as 'my God' in the same breath as He is asked why He has forgotten. A congregation that sings this psalm learns to bring its questions into praise, not to leave them at the door, and to keep singing while the answer is still delayed.

crossReferences.note: David, in a dry and weary land, says his soul thirsts and his body yearns for God. It has the same image of thirst as Psalm 42:1-2, but in a wilderness rather than beside water. The two psalms together show that thirst for God is the common experience of the faithful in every landscape.

Another Korahite psalm, in which the soul 'longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD' and the heart and flesh cry out for the living God. The phrase 'living God' matches Psalm 42:2, and the longing for the sanctuary answers the poet's memory of the procession in 42:4.

Jonah prays from inside the fish, 'all Your breakers and waves swept over me'. His words echo Psalm 42:7 almost exactly, showing how later worshippers borrowed the psalm's sea to describe their own distress. It also connects the psalm to Jesus, who takes Jonah as the sign of His burial and rising, Matthew 12:40.

The psalmist says he waits for the Lord and puts his hope in His word. It uses the same verb for hope as the refrain of Psalm 42:5, and shows that hope in the psalms is a waiting on God's word rather than a feeling of optimism.

The mockers say of the righteous sufferer, 'He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him'. Like the taunt of Psalm 42:3, it insults faith by pointing to unanswered prayer. Matthew 27:43 applies its words to Jesus on the cross.

Hannah, misjudged by Eli, says that she has poured out her soul before the Lord. Her idiom is the same as Psalm 42:4, and her story shows the outcome the poet hopes for: a grieving worshipper at the sanctuary who leaves with her face no longer sad, 1 Samuel 1:18.

On the last day of the feast Jesus calls the thirsty to come to Him and drink, promising streams of living water. He speaks as the fulfilment of the thirst in Psalm 42:1-2. The setting, a festival of pilgrims at the temple, matches the procession the poet remembers.

In Gethsemane Jesus says His soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. It joins Psalm 42:5 and 42:11, where the soul is bowed down and disturbed, and it shows the Lord entering the experience the refrain addresses, so that believers do not sing the psalm alone.

The waters roar and foam in this psalm, using the same root that describes the soul's unease in Psalm 42:5. The neighbouring Korahite psalm answers the flood of 42:7 with a river whose streams delight the city of God, Psalm 46:4, and a God who is a refuge.

The Lamb will lead His people to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear. It fulfils the psalmist's thirst of 42:1-2 and his food of tears in 42:3, promising the day when longing is satisfied and grief ends.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 42 stands in the story at the point where the presence of God is known by memory and hope. In Eden, humanity walked with God, Genesis 3:8, and was then sent away from that presence. The whole Bible after that moment is the story of a thirsty humanity being brought home. The tabernacle and temple were gracious provisions, places where God promised to meet His people, and the psalmist is a man who has been shut out of them. His thirst is an echo of Eden's loss.

The psalm also fits the pattern of exile that shapes the Old Testament. Israel is carried away from the land, and the taunt 'Where is your God?' expresses the doubt of the nations and the fear of the people. The prophets promise return, and Psalm 43 begins that return in prayer. Yet the return under Ezra and Nehemiah brings a rebuilt temple that never carries the glory of the first, and the longing continues.

The longing is answered in Christ. The Word becomes flesh and dwells among us, John 1:14, and He says of Himself that the temple of His body will be raised, John 2:19-21. He offers the thirsty living water, John 7:37, and gives His Spirit so that streams flow from within. The church, which is now the temple of the Holy Spirit, is scattered as the psalmist was, and it lives among hostile neighbours, but it lives with the presence of God.

The story ends where the psalm hoped. In the new creation the redeemed 'will see His face', Revelation 22:4. The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1, and the Lamb leads His people to springs of living water and wipes away every tear, Revelation 7:17. The thirst of the deer is finally satisfied, and the food of tears is replaced by a feast. The refrain, 'I will yet praise Him', finds its last word in the great multitude who cry out in worship, Revelation 7:9-10.

sermon.title: Prayer of Thirst
sermon.why: Keller preaches on Psalm 42:1-43:5 as one continuous prayer, showing how the psalmist's practice of talking to his own soul rather than merely listening to it models honest, hope-filled lament for anyone walking through spiritual darkness or distance from God.

quiz.q: What image does the psalmist use in verse 1 to describe his soul's longing for God?

options.text: A deer panting intensely for streams of water.
options.note: The Hebrew arag describes the desperate panting of a thirst-stricken animal, pictured elsewhere only in drought conditions, Joel 1:20.

options.text: A bird flying freely through the sky.
options.note: The text specifically uses the image of a panting deer thirsting for water, not a flying bird.

options.text: A tree planted firmly by streams of water.
options.note: That image appears in Psalm 1:3; this psalm's image is a panting, thirsty deer, emphasizing desperate longing rather than stability.

options.text: A shepherd searching for lost sheep.
options.note: The psalm's image is of the soul itself thirsting like a deer, not a shepherd searching for sheep.

quiz.q: What taunt do the psalmist's enemies repeat, according to verses 3 and 10?

options.text: "Where is your God?"
options.note: This exact taunt, repeated twice, anticipates the strikingly similar mockery hurled at Jesus on the cross in Matthew 27:43.

options.text: "You will never see the temple again."
options.note: While related to his separation from the temple, the explicit repeated taunt quoted in the text is 'Where is your God?'

options.text: "Your God has blessed you too much."
options.note: The taunt mocks the apparent absence of God's help, not excessive blessing.

options.text: "Your enemies will show you mercy."
options.note: The taunt is hostile mockery about God's apparent absence, not a promise of mercy from enemies.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist do in response to his own downcast, despairing feelings, verses 5 and 11?

options.text: He directly addresses his own soul, questioning its despair and commanding it to hope in God.
options.note: This refrain, repeated at the end of each movement, models actively preaching hope to oneself rather than simply obeying one's feelings.

options.text: He simply agrees with his despair and gives up hope entirely.
options.note: The refrain explicitly commands the soul to hope in God rather than surrendering to despair.

options.text: He blames God directly for abandoning him with no further reflection.
options.note: While he does ask 'Why have You forgotten me?' in verse 9, the refrain moves beyond blame to a deliberate command to hope.

options.text: He ignores his feelings entirely and pretends to feel nothing.
options.note: The psalmist openly names his downcast feelings rather than denying them; he then addresses and challenges them, not ignores them.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's central taunt anticipate an event in the Gospels?

options.text: It anticipates the mockery hurled at Jesus on the cross, 'He trusts in God; let God rescue Him now,' Matthew 27:43.
options.note: The wording and mocking intent closely parallel this psalm's repeated taunt, 'Where is your God?'

options.text: It anticipates the disciples' confession of faith at Caesarea Philippi.
options.note: That confession, Matthew 16:16, is an affirmation of faith, not a taunt questioning God's presence.

options.text: It anticipates the angel's announcement at the empty tomb.
options.note: The angel's announcement is a proclamation of resurrection, not a hostile taunt about God's absence.

options.text: It anticipates the crowd's shouts of Hosanna at the triumphal entry.
options.note: Those shouts are praise and welcome, the opposite tone of the mocking taunt this psalm anticipates.

quiz.q: What memory does the psalmist recall in verse 4 that deepens his present sorrow?

options.text: Walking with the multitude, leading the procession to the house of God with shouts of joy and praise.
options.note: Remembering past festival worship intensifies his present grief at being separated from God's house.

options.text: A time of military victory over his enemies.
options.note: The specific memory recalled is of joyful temple worship and procession, not military victory.

options.text: A conversation with the enemies who now taunt him.
options.note: The memory is of joyful worship with the multitude, not any conversation with his current enemies.

options.text: His original calling as a shepherd.
options.note: The remembered scene is specifically temple worship and festival procession, not a shepherding memory.

questions: The psalmist describes his longing for God as a deer desperately panting for water. Would you describe your own current longing for God's presence as desperate thirst, or has it grown more casual? What might rekindle that thirst?

The psalmist's enemies taunt him with 'Where is your God?' during his hardest season. Have you faced a similar taunt, from others or from your own doubting heart, during a time when God's presence felt hidden?

Rather than simply obeying his despair, the psalmist directly addresses his own soul and commands it to hope. What would it look like this week to actively preach truth to your own downcast soul rather than just listening to how you feel?

The psalmist remembers past seasons of joyful worship even while presently grieving. How can remembering specific past experiences of God's nearness help sustain hope during a present season of spiritual dryness or distance?

This psalm's taunt anticipates the mockery Jesus endured on the cross. How does knowing that Christ Himself entered this exact kind of anguish and mockery change how you bring your own downcast soul to Him?

translationNotes.note: Pants renders arag, describing the desperate, physical panting of a thirst-stricken animal, used elsewhere only in Joel 1:20 of creatures crying out in drought.
Downcast renders shachach, bowed down or sunk low; the psalmist directly addresses this state in his own soul rather than simply submitting to it, a refrain repeated in verses 5, 11, and 43:5.
Deep calls to deep uses the roar of cataracts and crashing waves as an image of overwhelming affliction, while still naming the waters and waves as God's own, 'Your waterfalls,' 'Your breakers.'
